records.sourceFile: A mixed methods investigation into athletic trainer and dietitian's nutrition practices for sport-related concussion patients.pdf

paper.citation: Weber Rawlins ML, Valovich McLeod TC. A mixed methods investigation into athletic trainer and dietitian's nutrition practices for sport-related concussion patients. J Concussion 2023;7:1-12.
paper.abstract: This mixed-methods survey described how athletic trainers and dietitians use nutrition, through food and supplements, to prevent concussion and to manage patients after concussion, and the barriers reported by those who do not. Most athletic trainers did not use nutrition for prevention, while dietitians used nutrition practices more often than not. Lack of clinician knowledge and athlete compliance were commonly reported barriers.
paper.tldr: Few athletic trainers (2.7%) use nutrition to prevent concussion, though about half offer at least some nutrition advice after one; dietitians report these practices more often. Lack of clinician knowledge was the most common barrier for athletic trainers. The study describes practice and cannot show whether any nutrient helps concussion outcomes.
paper.methods: Convergent parallel mixed-methods design. An online survey was distributed through the NATA Research Survey Service, the CPSDA discussion board and social media. Open-ended responses were coded with consensual qualitative research methods and checked by an external auditor, multiple-choice items were summarised with descriptive statistics, and the new survey had expert face and content validity review but no reliability analysis.
paper.findings: Among athletic trainers who accessed the survey (n = 1,465), 2.7% (39) reported using nutrition to prevent concussion, 28.5% (418) offered post-concussion nutrition recommendations, and 4.8% (70) changed nutrition for patients after concussion. Among dietitians (n = 51), the matching figures were 33.3% (17), 56.9% (29) and 29.4% (15). Respondents most often named clinician knowledge (49.4% of athletic trainers, 9.8% of dietitians) and athlete compliance (26.3%, 9.8%) as reasons for not implementing prevention nutrition.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional and descriptive, the response rate was low (7.3% of athletic trainers contacted and 3.6% of dietitians accessed the survey), and only 25 dietitians completed it. The Discussion says most dietitians were Division I, but Table 1 shows 25.5% (13) in Division I with 51% not responding. No validated survey existed, so the team built one reviewed only for face and content validity, and the authors call for longitudinal intervention studies.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors note that the current literature does not support nutrition for concussion prevention or post-injury care, so staff should not present it as a proven treatment. Because hydration status can change concussion symptoms, the authors advise relying on other assessments or delaying return-to-activity decisions until the athlete is euhydrated if dehydration is suspected. Interprofessional collaboration emerged as a theme, and the authors suggest athletic trainers and dietitians work together on any concussion nutrition plan.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest that, until more is known about nutrition and concussion, nutrition efforts may be better focused on athletic performance and injury recovery in general. The survey did not measure performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study does not test any return-to-play intervention. The authors cite the FDA position that there is no scientific evidence nutrition changes allow athletes to return to activity sooner, so nutrition should not be presented as a way to speed return to play.

records.sourceFile: A potential role exists for nutritional interventions in the chronic phase of mild traumatic brain injury, concussion and sports-related concussion - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Ryan T, Nagle S, Daly E, Pearce AJ, Ryan L. A potential role exists for nutritional interventions in the chronic phase of mild traumatic brain injury, concussion and sports-related concussion: a systematic review. Nutrients 2023;15:3726.
paper.abstract: This systematic review, registered on PROSPERO and conducted to PRISMA guidance, searched five databases for nutrition or dietary interventions in adults with chronic symptoms (at least one month) after mild traumatic brain injury, concussion or sport-related concussion. Nine studies met the criteria, covering omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, Enzogenol, MLC901, a ketogenic diet and phytocannabinoids. Findings were narrative because of heterogeneity, and the authors conclude that higher-quality human trials are needed.
paper.tldr: Few human trials have tested nutrition for symptoms that persist after mild brain injury, and the nine studies identified were small and varied. Several interventions were safe and some symptoms improved, but the review cannot establish whether any nutrient speeds recovery.
paper.methods: Systematic review registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021277780) and conducted following PRISMA 2020. Five databases were searched (PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL and Cochrane), with the search first run in 2020 and updated in 2023, identifying 6,164 records. Screening was done by two researchers with a third reviewer for disagreements, study quality was rated with a modified Black and Downs tool (maximum 28 points), and heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.
paper.findings: The nine studies covered omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, Enzogenol, MLC901, a ketogenic diet and phytocannabinoids. Trials reported some benefits, including lower self-reported anxiety with melatonin (p = 0.006 in Grima et al.), better executive functioning and complex attention with MLC901 (36 participants randomised to it), and possible benefit to visual memory and symptoms with a ketogenic diet in 11 completers of a feasibility study. The two omega-3 studies were multi-component programmes without a randomised control, so effects cannot be attributed to omega-3; one melatonin trial (Kemp et al.) found no sleep improvement; and the average quality score was 18.6 of 28.
paper.limitations: Samples were small: the Kemp et al. melatonin crossover study had seven participants and no power calculation, and the ketogenic study was a feasibility study with 11 completers. Only one study ran a sensitivity analysis, four studies did not adjust adequately for confounding, and all studies reported positive effects, which the authors flag as possible publication bias. The review was limited to adults in the chronic phase, so the findings do not apply to children, to acute injury or to moderate and severe TBI, and several trials mixed in moderate and severe TBI cases.
paper.practicalImplications: Because the evidence is limited, staff should not present any of these nutrients as an established treatment for persistent concussion symptoms. The interventions were feasible and well tolerated in these studies, but doses varied widely and the ketogenic diet needed ongoing dietitian input, so any use should be coordinated with a dietitian and monitored. Staff should also note the side effects reported in the trials, including headache and sleep disturbance with Enzogenol and headache and itchiness with MLC901.
paper.athleteDev: The review reports no performance outcomes. Its trial in college athletes with a history of concussion (Walter et al.) tested Enzogenol for residual symptoms and reported improved sleep disturbance and mental fatigue, but it did not measure performance.
paper.rtp: The review measured symptoms, cognition, sleep and mood rather than return to play, and it does not identify an intervention that shortens recovery. Nutrition should therefore not be used to accelerate return to activity or to inform return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: Acute myocardial infarction following dry scooping of a pre-workout supplement in a healthy young man of African origin - A case report.pdf

paper.citation: Pallangyo P, Bhalia SV, Komba M, Mkojera ZS, Manji ES, Millinga J, et al. Acute myocardial infarction following "dry scooping" of a pre-workout supplement in a healthy young man of African origin: a case report. SAGE Open Medical Case Reports. 2024;12:1-6.
paper.abstract: A previously healthy 25-year-old man presented with chest pain after a gym session, having used a pre-workout supplement for 8 months and dry-scooped it for 3 days. He had an anterolateral STEMI from a thrombotic proximal LAD occlusion, treated with a drug-eluting stent, and the authors use the case to raise awareness of pre-workout misuse.
paper.tldr: Dry scooping a pre-workout powder preceded an acute heart attack in a healthy young gym user, whose coronary blockage was treated with a stent. The cause is uncertain, so the case supports warning against dry scooping but does not prove a mechanism.
paper.methods: Clinical case description covering history, ECG, echocardiography, coronary angiography, laboratory tests, treatment and follow-up at 4 weeks. Written consent for publication was obtained, and the institution did not require ethics approval for an individual case report.
paper.findings: Peak troponin I was 5.14 ng/mL and CK-MB 78.1 ng/mL. Angiography showed a thrombotic total occlusion of the proximal LAD with TIMI 0 flow and no atherosclerosis, restored to TIMI 3 flow by stenting, and coagulation and lipid tests were unremarkable. At 4 weeks he reported normal functional capacity with a normal ECG, and echocardiography showed preserved EF with limited residual anterior hypokinesia; the authors suggest pre-workout-induced coronary spasm as a possible but unproven cause.
paper.limitations: This is one patient, with no testing of the supplement content and no test for coronary spasm. The authors acknowledge that the cause of the thrombus remains uncertain, so the spasm explanation is speculative.
paper.practicalImplications: The case supports advising gym users and athletes not to dry scoop pre-workout powder, and asking about supplement use when a young person presents with chest pain. It does not establish how often dry scooping causes harm or the risk for any specific product.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the case is a reason to ask athletes about pre-workout and stimulant use, especially dry scooping and high-caffeine products. It cannot be used to estimate how common the risk is.
paper.rtp: The case does not give return-to-sport criteria. It reports normal functional capacity, a normal ECG and limited residual anterior wall hypokinesia at 4 weeks after stenting, but this is one patient and no return-to-exercise decision is described.

records.sourceFile: Adulteration of sports supplements with anabolic steroids - From innocent athlete to vicious cheater.pdf

paper.citation: Puscasiu D, Flangea C, Vlad D, Popescu R, Vlad CS, Barac S, et al. Adulteration of Sports Supplements with Anabolic Steroids-From Innocent Athlete to Vicious Cheater. Nutrients. 2025;17:3146.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers two situations: an athlete who tests positive after unknowingly taking a supplement adulterated with anabolic steroids, and an athlete who uses steroids and masks them. It describes testosterone synthesis and metabolism, the WADA steroid profile markers, isotope ratio mass spectrometry, and masking agents such as finasteride, probenecid, diuretics and azole antifungals.
paper.tldr: Protein and other supplements can contain undeclared anabolic steroids, so an athlete can test positive without intending to dope. This review explains the steroid profile markers and masking agents that anti-doping labs use, and it says medical staff should recommend only contamination-free supplements.
paper.methods: Narrative review drawing on PubMed, Google Scholar and ScienceDirect, including review articles, original research, case reports, meta-analyses and current WADA documents. Conference abstracts, letters, editorials and comments without peer review were excluded. No systematic search protocol or formal quality assessment is described.
paper.findings: The review reports that earlier studies identified 54, 67 and 93 steroid substances in protein supplements, that 52.2% of supplements in one study were contaminated with anabolic steroids, and that 25 of 66 supplements in another contained prohibited substances. It sets out WADA screening thresholds, including urinary testosterone above 200 ng/mL in men, a testosterone to epitestosterone ratio above 4, and an isotope ratio difference above 3 per mil as indicating exogenous steroid use. It also describes masking agents that change the steroid profile, for example finasteride combined with 19-norandrostenedione lowering urinary norandrosterone by up to 84%, ketoconazole reducing urinary testosterone, androsterone, etiocholanolone and the testosterone to epitestosterone ratio, and miconazole reducing androsterone and etiocholanolone.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review without a systematic search or appraisal of study quality, so the selection of evidence may be biased. Many cited mechanistic and masking data come from small studies, including animal work, and the review does not report new human data. The adulteration figures are from earlier product testing and may not reflect current supplements.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should treat supplements, especially protein products, as a possible source of undeclared steroids; the authors say medical staff should recommend only contamination-free supplements and athletes should use supplements under sports medicine supervision. Medical staff should coordinate prescribed medications such as anxiolytics and antidepressants with anti-doping rules. Athletes are judged on the test result regardless of intent, so they should be told this.
paper.athleteDev: Supplements that promise rapid strength or muscle gains deserve extra scrutiny, because the review describes undeclared steroids being added to protein products to drive sales, and a positive test can end a career. The review supports using only controlled supplements recommended by medical staff; it does not test or rank specific products.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not study injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play clearance, and its doping and supplement content should not be used to judge an athlete's readiness to play.
